title: Sample-optimal Gaussian graphical model learning in polynomial time
formal: Can general Gaussian conditional-independence graphs be learned in uniform polynomial time using, up to a universal constant factor, the information-theoretically optimal number of independent observations? For integers \(p\ge2\), \(1\le d\le p-1\), \(r\ge2\), and rational \(0<\kappa<1\), let \(\mathcal G(p,d,\kappa)\) be the Gaussian family defined below and let \(m^*(p,d,\kappa,r)\) be its minimax sample count for exact graph recovery with failure probability at most \(2^{-r}\), allowing unrestricted measurable estimators. Is there one uniform randomized algorithm \(A\) and constants \(C,B,a\ge1\) such that, for every parameter choice and every \(P\in\mathcal G(p,d,\kappa)\), \(A(p,d,\kappa,r)\) returns its exact graph with probability at least \(1-2^{-r}\), draws at most \(\lceil C m^*(p,d,\kappa,r)\rceil\) independent samples, and uses at most \[B\bigl(p+d+\lceil\kappa^{-1}\rceil+r+L\bigr)^a\] real-arithmetic operations, including sample loading and output, where \(L\) is the binary encoding length of \(\kappa\)? The exponent and constants must be independent of every parameter and of the unknown distribution. This retains the general sample-optimal computational question from the source’s conclusion; bounded-degree recovery is already treated there. The minimax definition does not presume that the commonly quoted \(d\log p/\kappa^2\) sample scale is sharp in all joint parameter regimes.

source_formulation.text: Can the information-theoretically optimal independent-sample count for general Gaussian graph recovery be attained by a polynomial-time algorithm?
source_formulation.caption: Editorial paraphrase

why: Sparse conditional dependence can be statistically identifiable even when variables are extremely correlated. Recovering that graph from few observations is useful only if the necessary search is computationally affordable. The problem asks whether uniformly efficient computation must pay an extra sample cost without regularity assumptions on the covariance.
status_note: The source already gives sample-efficient polynomial-time recovery for bounded degree, but with a degree-dependent runtime exponent. Its p4 discussion qualifies the claimed information-theoretic matching when degree and minimum edge strength vary together. The residual general question is therefore stated using a defined minimax independent-sample count, not an assumed uniformly tight d log p / kappa² formula. COLT 2024 Remark 43 gives a conditional statistical-computational gap under Conjecture 33; that assumption is not asserted true. A 2026 primary paper still distinguishes the independent-sample difficulty while solving a different Glauber-trajectory problem. No unconditional resolution of the displayed uniform arithmetic-time target was checked through 16 September 2026. Numerical precision and cross-model hardness transfers are explicitly not certified.

progress.text: DICE proves an explicit sample upper bound independent of condition number; its degree-dependent search is polynomial for bounded degree, with a stated caveat about statistical tightness for joint degree/strength scaling.
Fixed polynomial-time recovery without condition-number assumptions is obtained for attractive and walk-summable subclasses.
Remark 43 derives a GGM statistical-computational separation conditional on the specific low-degree/spiked-Wishart detection conjecture.
A new polynomial-time result uses a Glauber trajectory; the paper distinguishes the unresolved independent-sample problem.
Rechecked the source’s theorem, caveat and final question; retained the unrestricted model, minimax sample definition and conditional nature of later hardness evidence.

importance.reason: A basic statistical-computational question for sparse Gaussian models, distinguished by the absence of spectral assumptions and the exact graph-recovery objective; it now has substantive conditional separation evidence.

sentences: The problem asks whether sparse Gaussian conditional-independence graphs can be recovered in polynomial time with an information-theoretically optimal number of independent samples.
The statement allows arbitrary means and condition numbers and requires every edge and nonedge to be identified correctly.
Sample optimality is defined by a minimax benchmark that retains degree, normalized edge strength and confidence without assuming a universally sharp formula.
Known degree-dependent algorithms, structural-subclass results, conditional hardness and trajectory-based algorithms each address a different part of the question.
A Lean resolution must establish or refute one uniform algorithm with both a universal sample factor and a fixed polynomial arithmetic-time bound.

definitions:
A member \(P\) of \(\mathcal G(p,d,\kappa)\) is \(N(\mu,\Sigma)\), where \(\mu\in\mathbb R^p\) is arbitrary, \(\Sigma\) is a real symmetric positive definite \(p\times p\) covariance matrix, and \(\Theta=\Sigma^{-1}\) is its precision matrix. Its undirected graph has vertices \([p]=\{1,\ldots,p\}\) and an edge \(\{i,j\}\), for \(i\ne j\), exactly when \(\Theta_{ij}\ne0\). Every vertex has at most \(d\) neighbors, and every edge satisfies \[\frac{|\Theta_{ij}|}{\sqrt{\Theta_{ii}\Theta_{jj}}}\ge\kappa.\] This normalized precision entry is the magnitude of the corresponding partial correlation. For an empty graph the edge condition holds vacuously. The parameters are upper and lower promises, not assertions that degree equals \(d\) or minimum strength equals \(\kappa\). No eigenvalue, condition-number, variance, sign-pattern, incoherence, faithfulness, treewidth or walk-summability restriction is imposed. The learner is not given \(\mu,\Sigma,\Theta\), or a graph representation.

An observation is an entire vector \(X\in\mathbb R^p\) drawn from \(P\); observations are independent and identically distributed. The graph-recovery loss is zero exactly when all off-diagonal zero/nonzero decisions are correct, and one otherwise. Estimating covariance entries to a numerical tolerance is a different task. The probability in the guarantee includes the observations and internal randomness. The public failure tolerance is \(2^{-r}\); allowing all integers \(r\ge2\) keeps confidence variable. The graph output is its \(p\times p\) symmetric binary adjacency matrix with zero diagonal.

For a fixed \((p,d,\kappa,r)\), define \(m^*\) as the least nonnegative integer \(m\) for which some Borel-measurable randomized estimator from \((\mathbb R^p)^m\) to the finite set of labeled undirected graphs satisfies \[\inf_{P\in\mathcal G(p,d,\kappa)}\Pr_{X_1,\ldots,X_m\sim P}[\widehat G(X_1,\ldots,X_m)=G(P)]\ge1-2^{-r}.\] Randomization is an independent infinite fair-bit sequence, and the estimator must be measurable jointly in data and that sequence. It may depend arbitrarily on the four public parameters and has no computation bound; this defines an information benchmark, not a computational oracle. If the set of such sample counts were empty, set \(m^*=+\infty\); known finite sample upper bounds exclude that case for this family. The target algorithm receives neither \(m^*\) nor an optimal estimator. Its sample limit must hold on every possible observation and coin history, even if it adaptively decides when to stop. Padding an early stop with unused observations makes comparison with fixed-size estimators unambiguous.

Computation uses an explicitly chosen standard exact-real arithmetic convention. One finite uniform register program has rational constants in its code, discrete control and fair random bits. Copying, \(+,-,\times,\div\), comparison, branching and each control or output operation cost one unit; any division must be guarded at a zero denominator. Loading one observed vector costs \(p\) units. The algorithm outputs only finite bits for the adjacency matrix. It has no access to conditional samples, a Markov transition trajectory, matrix entries of the unknown distribution, exact expectations, optimization oracles, arbitrary real advice, floor/digit extraction, or an oracle deciding general real-number properties. The positive integers \(p,d,r\) are public unary inputs and \(\kappa\) is supplied by positive coprime binary numerator and denominator, with total bit length \(L\). Reading and translating these inputs are counted. The displayed worst-case operation bound applies to all sample and random-bit histories, not just in expectation.

This convention makes the source’s continuous-observation computational question precise without asserting equivalence to finite-bit Gaussian data. Exact Gaussian coordinates are generally not finite binary strings; the source does not prescribe a rounding budget. In particular, allowing arbitrary condition numbers in the distribution is material to numerical implementation. Any finite-precision result, or computational hardness assumption in another machine model, needs a justified relation to this arithmetic convention before it resolves the displayed proposition. Polynomial time means a single fixed exponent for variable \(d\); \(p^{O(d)}\) is insufficient. Sample optimality means a universal multiplicative factor, with no suppressed dependence on \(d,\kappa,r\) or logarithmic loss.
answer_criterion: Give a Lean proof of the existence proposition or its full negation. An affirmative result must supply one uniform algorithm and constants, prove exact graph recovery over the entire promised Gaussian family, prove the universal constant-factor comparison with the defined information-theoretic minimum, and verify worst-case sample and arithmetic-time bounds. A negative result must rule out every such learner and constants on some allowed parameters or distribution. A conditional computational obstruction remains conditional unless its hypothesis is also proved. A \(p^{O(d)}\) method, a result only for a fixed degree, a polynomial-time method using more than a universal-factor sample overhead, or a theorem with extra spectral/sign assumptions does not suffice. Neither does learning from a Glauber trajectory establish the independent-observation guarantee. A closed form for \(m^*\) is useful but is not assumed in advance; any claimed closed form must be proved uniformly in its stated regime. The answer is an exact yes/no theorem, not a numerical estimate of a covariance matrix.

context_blocks.text: The graph records conditional dependence, not merely pairwise correlation: an edge is determined by a nonzero entry of the inverse covariance matrix. Strong correlations and poor conditioning are allowed. This explains why guarantees depending only on dimension, sparsity and normalized edge strength are stronger than many familiar covariance-estimation results.

The source’s DICE theorem gives exact recovery when \(m>2d+192\kappa^{-2}d\log p+64\kappa^{-2}\log(4d/\delta)\). Its neighborhood-search cost is \(O(p^{2d+1})\). Thus fixed-degree graphs have a polynomial-time guarantee, but the exponent is not uniform over growing degree.

The source explicitly qualifies statistical tightness when degree grows while minimum edge strength shrinks. Therefore its motivating abstract sentence cannot be read as an unresolved bounded-degree theorem, or its sample bound as a universally matching minimax formula. The current question retains the general computational issue using an explicit minimax benchmark.

Kelner–Koehler–Meka–Moitra provide fixed polynomial-time algorithms without condition-number bounds for attractive and walk-summable Gaussian models. These are genuine positive results for additional structural subclasses. Their assumptions do not cover every signed precision matrix in the present family.

COLT 2024 Kelner–Koehler–Meka–Rohatgi, Remark 43, gives conditional evidence of a sample-computation gap. Under its Conjecture 33 relating low-degree likelihood tests to polynomial-time detection for a spiked Wishart model, efficient general recovery would need nearly quadratic rather than linear dependence on sparsity in the relevant regime, even at constant normalized edge strength. The conjecture is not a proved theorem about arbitrary algorithms.

The hard family in that remark has covariance equal to identity plus a negative rank-one perturbation supported on a hidden sparse set. Exact graph recovery would distinguish it from the independent-coordinate null model. This is a stated reduction under a specific detection-hardness conjecture, not an unconditional archive-worthy impossibility. Its computational convention must also match any use against the real-arithmetic target.

The 2026 Shen–Wu–Majid–Moitra paper gives a polynomial-time method observing one Glauber trajectory, where coordinates are successively resampled conditional on the others. Its introduction still identifies efficient recovery from few independent samples as unresolved. A trajectory exposes update information that independent observations do not provide, so the newer theorem does not automatically answer the present question.
